claim: Spindle length scales with cell size in C. elegans embryos during development.
source: During early embryogenesis in C. elegans, X. laevis and various metazoans where cell size gradually decreases while the embryo undergoes successive rounds of cell division, spindle length can be reduced from 60 to a few micrometers (Crowder et al., 2015; Hara and Kimura, 2009; Wühr et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Crowder et al., 2015; Hara and Kimura, 2009; Wühr et al., 2008).

claim: Spindle length scales with cell size in X. laevis embryos during development.
source: During early embryogenesis in C. elegans, X. laevis and various metazoans where cell size gradually decreases while the embryo undergoes successive rounds of cell division, spindle length can be reduced from 60 to a few micrometers (Crowder et al., 2015; Hara and Kimura, 2009; Wühr et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Crowder et al., 2015; Hara and Kimura, 2009; Wühr et al., 2008).

claim: Spindle length adjusts to cell size in S. cerevisiae.
source: Also apart from embryogenesis, spindle length has been shown to adjust to cell size in S. cerevisiae and human cells (Rizk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Rizk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).

claim: Spindle length adjusts to cell size in human cells.
source: Also apart from embryogenesis, spindle length has been shown to adjust to cell size in S. cerevisiae and human cells (Rizk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Rizk et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2016).

claim: The relationship between spindle length and cell size is regulated by cytoplasmic volume through limiting cytoplasmic components such as tubulin.
source: This relationship is regulated by the cytoplasmic volume through limiting cytoplasmic components, such as tubulin (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013), as well as by molecules modulating microtubule dynamics (Hara and Kimura, 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Reber and Goehring, 2015; Wilbur and Heald, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013).

claim: The relationship between spindle length and cell size is regulated by molecules modulating microtubule dynamics.
source: This relationship is regulated by the cytoplasmic volume through limiting cytoplasmic components, such as tubulin (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013), as well as by molecules modulating microtubule dynamics (Hara and Kimura, 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Reber and Goehring, 2015; Wilbur and Heald, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hara and Kimura, 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Reber and Goehring, 2015; Wilbur and Heald, 2013).

claim: In C. elegans embryos, the velocity of spindle assembly in prophase adjusts to cell size.
source: In C. elegans embryos, the velocity of spindle assembly in prophase and the velocity of spindle elongation in anaphase B adjust to cell size, such that longer spindles assemble and elongate with proportionally higher speeds (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Lacroix et al., 2018).

claim: In C. elegans embryos, the velocity of spindle elongation in anaphase B adjusts to cell size.
source: In C. elegans embryos, the velocity of spindle assembly in prophase and the velocity of spindle elongation in anaphase B adjust to cell size, such that longer spindles assemble and elongate with proportionally higher speeds (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Lacroix et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Lacroix et al., 2018).

claim: Prolongation of mitosis results in cell death or arrest in subsequent cell cycle phases.
source: In fact, prolongation of mitosis has often been shown to result in cell death or arrest in subsequent cell cycle phases (Araujo et al., 2016; Lanni and Jacks, 1998; Orth et al., 2012; Quignon et al., 2007; Rieder and Palazzo, 1992; Uetake and Sluder, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Araujo et al., 2016; Lanni and Jacks, 1998; Orth et al., 2012; Quignon et al., 2007; Rieder and Palazzo, 1992; Uetake and Sluder, 2010).

claim: Computer simulations suggest that cell-size-dependent spindle elongation velocity in C. elegans embryos depends on the number of cortical force-generators pulling on spindle poles.
source: Computer simulations suggest that the cell-size-dependent spindle elongation velocity in C. elegans embryos depends on the number of cortical force-generators pulling on spindle poles (Hara and Kimura, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Hara and Kimura, 2009).

claim: Many organisms push spindle poles apart via microtubule sliding forces generated between antiparallel overlapping microtubules at the spindle midzone.
source: In contrast to this mechanism of anaphase B, many other organisms push spindle poles apart via microtubule sliding forces generated between antiparallel overlapping microtubules (MTs) at the spindle center (spindle midzone) (Brust-Mascher et al., 2004; Brust-Mascher and Scholey, 2011; Hayashi et al., 2007; Khodjakov et al., 2004; Tolić-Nørrelykke et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Brust-Mascher et al., 2004; Brust-Mascher and Scholey, 2011; Hayashi et al., 2007; Khodjakov et al., 2004; Tolić-Nørrelykke et al., 2004).

claim: In most organisms, microtubule sliding forces are generated by kinesin-5.
source: In most organisms, these forces are generated by kinesin-5 (Avunie-Masala et al., 2011; Brust-Mascher et al., 2009; Kapitein et al., 2008; Kapitein et al., 2005; Saunders et al., 1995; Sharp et al., 2000) but also kinesin-6, as in fission yeast, can accomplish this task (Fu et al., 2009; Rincon et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Avunie-Masala et al., 2011; Brust-Mascher et al., 2009; Kapitein et al., 2008; Kapitein et al., 2005; Saunders et al., 1995; Sharp et al., 2000).

claim: Kinesin-6 can generate microtubule sliding forces in fission yeast.
source: In most organisms, these forces are generated by kinesin-5 (Avunie-Masala et al., 2011; Brust-Mascher et al., 2009; Kapitein et al., 2008; Kapitein et al., 2005; Saunders et al., 1995; Sharp et al., 2000) but also kinesin-6, as in fission yeast, can accomplish this task (Fu et al., 2009; Rincon et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Fu et al., 2009; Rincon et al., 2017).

claim: Forces generated by several kinesin-5 molecules that crosslink and slide apart antiparallel overlapping microtubules add up in vitro.
source: In vitro it has been shown that the forces generated by several kinesin-5 molecules, that crosslink and slide apart antiparallel overlapping microtubules add up (Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Shimamoto et al., 2015).

claim: In fission yeast, cell growth only occurs at cell tips and the diameter does not change.
source: In the rod-shaped fission yeast, cell growth only occurs at cell tips and the diameter does not change (Kelly and Nurse, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kelly and Nurse, 2011).

claim: wee1-50 mutant cells divide at an abnormally short cell length of 10.50 µm ± 1 µm.
source: To investigate the impact of cell size on mitotic spindle length and mitosis duration, we used cell-cycle mutants, dividing at an abnormally short (wee1-50: 10.50 µm ± 1 µm) and abnormally long cell length (cdc25-22: 24.7 µm ± 2.6 µm) compared to wild-type cells (13.3 µm ± 0.7 µm) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: cdc25-22 mutant cells divide at an abnormally long cell length of 24.7 µm ± 2.6 µm.
source: To investigate the impact of cell size on mitotic spindle length and mitosis duration, we used cell-cycle mutants, dividing at an abnormally short (wee1-50: 10.50 µm ± 1 µm) and abnormally long cell length (cdc25-22: 24.7 µm ± 2.6 µm) compared to wild-type cells (13.3 µm ± 0.7 µm) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: Wild-type S. pombe cells divide at a cell length of 13.3 µm ± 0.7 µm.
source: To investigate the impact of cell size on mitotic spindle length and mitosis duration, we used cell-cycle mutants, dividing at an abnormally short (wee1-50: 10.50 µm ± 1 µm) and abnormally long cell length (cdc25-22: 24.7 µm ± 2.6 µm) compared to wild-type cells (13.3 µm ± 0.7 µm) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1A and Figure 1—source data 1).

claim: Short wee1-50 cells assemble spindles with a maximum length of 10.14 ± 1.2 µm.
source: Short wee1-50 cells assembled spindles with a maximum length of 10.14 ± 1.2 µm, wild-type cells of 11.93 ± 0.9 µm and long cdc25-22 cells of 17.34 ± 1.4 µm on average (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1C and D).

claim: Wild-type S. pombe cells assemble spindles with a maximum length of 11.93 ± 0.9 µm.
source: Short wee1-50 cells assembled spindles with a maximum length of 10.14 ± 1.2 µm, wild-type cells of 11.93 ± 0.9 µm and long cdc25-22 cells of 17.34 ± 1.4 µm on average (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1C and D).

claim: Long cdc25-22 cells assemble spindles with a maximum length of 17.34 ± 1.4 µm.
source: Short wee1-50 cells assembled spindles with a maximum length of 10.14 ± 1.2 µm, wild-type cells of 11.93 ± 0.9 µm and long cdc25-22 cells of 17.34 ± 1.4 µm on average (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1C and D).

claim: Maximum spindle length increases in proportion to cell size in S. pombe with R2 = 0.94 and slope m = 0.49.
source: This shows that maximum spindle length increased in proportion to cell size (Figure 1D: R2 = 0.94, m = 0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Metaphase spindle length scales with cell size in S. pombe with R2 = 0.6 and slope m = 0.07.
source: Metaphase spindle length, measured at the end of metaphase (Figure 1B: phase II-arrowhead), also scaled with cell size, although to a slightly lower extent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1: R2 = 0.6, m = 0.07).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Total spindle duration is constant among S. pombe cells of different sizes, taking place within approximately 30 min.
source: Consequently, total spindle duration, that is the time from the appearance of the spindle until its breakdown (Figure 1B), was constant among cells of different sizes, taking place within approximately 30 min (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1E.

claim: Total spindle duration is independent of cell size in S. pombe with R2 = 0.02 and slope m = 0.06.
source: Total spindle duration, which we define as mitosis duration, was thus independent of cell size (Figure 1E: R2 = 0.02, m = 0.06).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 1E.

claim: The velocity of spindle elongation in anaphase B increases with cell size in S. pombe.
source: This is achieved by an increase of the spindle elongation velocity with cell size. The scaling relationship of spindle dynamics and cell size was observed in all mitotic phases (Figure 1—figure supplement 2): the rate of spindle assembly in prophase, the velocity of very modest spindle elongation in metaphase and, most strikingly, the velocity of extensive spindle elongation in anaphase B increased with cell size (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rate of spindle assembly in prophase increases with cell size in S. pombe.
source: The scaling relationship of spindle dynamics and cell size was observed in all mitotic phases (Figure 1—figure supplement 2): the rate of spindle assembly in prophase, the velocity of very modest spindle elongation in metaphase and, most strikingly, the velocity of extensive spindle elongation in anaphase B increased with cell size (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The velocity of spindle elongation in metaphase increases with cell size in S. pombe.
source: The scaling relationship of spindle dynamics and cell size was observed in all mitotic phases (Figure 1—figure supplement 2): the rate of spindle assembly in prophase, the velocity of very modest spindle elongation in metaphase and, most strikingly, the velocity of extensive spindle elongation in anaphase B increased with cell size (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Abnormally short cells were obtained by growing wild-type cells under conditions of starvation, which divide at an average cell length of 10.91 ± 0.95 µm.
source: Abnormally short cells were obtained by growing wild-type cells under conditions of starvation, which then divide at an average cell length of 10.91 ± 0.95 µm (Figure 2A: starved wt).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Wild-type cells treated with hydroxyurea enter mitosis at an average length of 15.73 ± 0.95 µm.
source: Abnormally long cells were created by, first, treatment of wild-type cells with hydroxyurea (HU), which allows to arrest them in early S-Phase by disturbing DNA replication. After a few hours of incubation the drug can be washed out, allowing the cells to resume the cell cycle and enter mitosis at an average length of 15.73 ± 0.95 µm (Figure 2A: wt +HU).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: cdc2-asM17 cells treated with NM-PP1 divide at cell lengths ranging from 12.24 to 27.09 µm depending on the duration of incubation.
source: Depending on the duration of incubation with the ATP-analogue inhibitor NM-PP1, cdc2-asM17 cells divided at cell lengths ranging from 12.24 to 27.09 µm (Figure 2A: cdc2-asM17 + NMPP1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: In S. pombe, outward sliding of antiparallel microtubules is predominantly executed by the kinesin-6 Klp9.
source: In S. pombe, outward sliding of antiparallel microtubules is predominantly executed by the kinesin-6 Klp9 (Figure 3C) (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fu et al., 2009) and Figure 3C.

claim: Ase1 bundles antiparallel microtubules at anaphase onset, organizing the spindle midzone.
source: At anaphase onset the highly conserved MT-crosslinker Ase1 (PRC1/MAP65) bundles antiparallel microtubules, organizing a structure of overlapping microtubules that is called spindle midzone (Bieling et al., 2010; Gaillard et al., 2008; Glotzer, 2009; Janson et al., 2007; Loïodice et al., 2005; Mollinari et al., 2002; Pellman et al., 1995; Schuyler et al., 2003; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bieling et al., 2010; Gaillard et al., 2008; Glotzer, 2009; Janson et al., 2007; Loïodice et al., 2005; Mollinari et al., 2002; Pellman et al., 1995; Schuyler et al., 2003; Yamashita et al., 2005).

claim: Ase1 recruits Klp9 to the midzone in a dephosphorylation-dependent manner.
source: In this position, Ase1 is thought to recruit Klp9, which is localized to the nucleus, in a dephosphorylation-dependent manner to the midzone (Figure 3B and C) (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Fu et al., 2009) and Figures 3B and C.

claim: Klp9 is a plus-end directed homotetrameric motor that can slide apart antiparallel microtubules and elongate the mitotic spindle.
source: As a plus-end directed homotetrameric motor, Klp9 can slide apart the antiparallel microtubules and elongate the mitotic spindle (Fu et al., 2009; Rincon et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Fu et al., 2009; Rincon et al., 2017).

claim: Deletion of Klp9 decreases the speed of anaphase B spindle elongation velocity in wee1-50, wild-type and cdc25-22 cells.
source: Deletion of Klp9 decreased the speed of anaphase B spindle elongation velocity in wee1-50, wild-type and cdc25-22 cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Anaphase spindle elongation velocities in klp9Δ cells range between 0.3–0.5 µm/min in all three cell types.
source: Strikingly, anaphase spindle elongation velocities decreased to very similar values in all three cell types (Figure 3D and E), as well as in the cdc2-asM17 mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), ranging between 0.3–0.5 µm/min.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3D, E, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlation between spindle elongation velocity and cell size is abolished in absence of Klp9.
source: Thus, the correlation between spindle elongation velocity and cell size is abolished in absence of Klp9.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar velocities in klp9Δ cells of different sizes.

claim: The scaling relationship of spindle length and cell size is maintained in absence of Klp9.
source: Despite this, the scaling relationship of spindle length and cell size was still effective (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In absence of Klp9, longer cells need proportionally more time to complete chromosome segregation compared to shorter cells.
source: As a result of similar spindle elongation velocities in the absence of Klp9, longer cells needed proportionally more time to complete chromosome segregation compared to shorter cells (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phenomenon of constant mitosis duration irrespective of cell size is abolished in absence of Klp9.
source: Thus, the phenomenon of constant mitosis duration irrespective of cell size is abolished in absence of Klp9.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mitosis duration correlates with cell size in klp9Δ cells.

claim: Kinesin-6 Klp9 is a key component of the mechanism that adjusts spindle elongation velocity to cell size.
source: Together, these results suggest that the kinesin-6 Klp9 is a key component of the mechanism that adjusts spindle elongation velocity to cell size.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that deletion of Klp9 abolishes the scaling relationship between spindle elongation velocity and cell size.

claim: Klp9-GFP intensity at the midzone increases from wee1-50 to wild-type to cdc25-22 cells at every given time point during anaphase B.
source: In general, the Klp9-GFP intensity increased from wee1-50 to wild-type to cdc25-22 cells at every given time point (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Total Klp9-GFP intensity in cells increases with cell size.
source: Moreover, in addition to the Klp9-GFP intensity at the midzone of anaphase spindles (Figure 4C: unfilled dots) also the total Klp9-GFP intensity in cells (Figure 4C: filled dots), measured shortly before mitosis onset within the nucleus, increased with cell size (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: Klp9-GFP intensity at anaphase spindles increases with cell size.
source: Moreover, in addition to the Klp9-GFP intensity at the midzone of anaphase spindles (Figure 4C: unfilled dots) also the total Klp9-GFP intensity in cells (Figure 4C: filled dots), measured shortly before mitosis onset within the nucleus, increased with cell size (Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4C and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: Approximately 40% of the total cellular Klp9 pool is recruited to anaphase spindles in all cell types.
source: More precisely, approximately 40% of the total cellular Klp9 pool was recruited to anaphase spindles in all cell types (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Klp9 spindle fraction (ratio of Klp9-GFP intensity at anaphase spindles over total intensity) does not correlate with cell size with R2 = 0.08 and slope m = 0.0015.
source: The latter is supported by the fact that the ratio of Klp9-GFP intensity at anaphase spindles over its total intensity in the cell, referred to as Klp9 spindle fraction, did not correlate with cell size (Figure 4D: R2 = 0.08, m = 0.0015; and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Klp9 concentration in the cell is largely independent of cell size with R2 = 0.09 and slope m = −0.02.
source: Indeed, we found the Klp9 concentration in the cell to be largely independent of cell size (Figure 4E: R2 = 0.09, m = −0.02 and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 4E and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The total amount of tubulin within the cell increases proportional to cell size.
source: Similarly to the quantities of Klp9, we observed, that the amount of tubulin, either the total amount of tubulin within the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 4: filled dots) or the amount of tubulin incorporated within the late anaphase spindle (Figure 4—figure supplement 4: unfilled dots) increased proportional to cell size.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The amount of tubulin incorporated within the late anaphase spindle increases proportional to cell size.
source: Similarly to the quantities of Klp9, we observed, that the amount of tubulin, either the total amount of tubulin within the cell (Figure 4—figure supplement 4: filled dots) or the amount of tubulin incorporated within the late anaphase spindle (Figure 4—figure supplement 4: unfilled dots) increased proportional to cell size.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The concentration of tubulin in the cell remains constant in cells of different sizes.
source: Furthermore the concentration of tubulin in the cell, estimated by the ratio of total mCherry-Atb2 intensity and cell volume, remained constant in cells of different sizes (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Anaphase B spindle elongation velocity is altered in a dose-dependent manner relative to the expression level of klp9.
source: Anaphase B spindle elongation velocity was altered in a dose-dependent manner relative to the expression level of klp9 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The stronger klp9 is overexpressed, the faster anaphase spindles elongate.
source: Generally, the stronger klp9 was overexpressed, the faster anaphase spindles elongated (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: GFP-klp9 intensities at anaphase spindles increase in proportion to expression levels.
source: Intensity measurements in cells expressing GFP-klp9 under the control of the different nmt promoters revealed an increase of GFP-klp9 intensities, measured in anaphase spindles, in proportion to expression levels (Figure 5E and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5E and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: An increase of GFP-klp9 signal on the spindle correlates with an increase of spindle elongation velocity until an upper-limit of approximately 1.1–1.2 µm/min.
source: An increase of GFP-klp9 signal on the spindle correlates with an increase of spindle elongation velocity until a certain upper-limit (Figure 5D). At a velocity of approximately 1.1–1.2 µm/min no strong acceleration occurred even though GFP-klp9 intensities increased further (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Ase1 localizes to the midzone shortly before anaphase onset and stays at the midzone as well as at spindle poles throughout anaphase B.
source: Ase1 localizes to the midzone shortly before anaphase onset (Figure 6A: arrowhead) and stays at the midzone as well as at spindle poles throughout anaphase B, as previously reported (Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A and citations to published research (Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005).

claim: Ase1-GFP intensity at the spindle midzone increases proportional to cell size.
source: Intensity measurements in wild-type, wee1-50 and cdc25-22 cells expressing Ase1-GFP revealed an increase at the spindle midzone proportional to cell size (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: Expression of ase1 under the control of pnmt81 and pnmt41 decreases anaphase B spindle elongation velocity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Expression of ase1 under the control of pnmt81 and pnmt41 decreased anaphase B spindle elongation velocity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Ase1 acts as a brake opposing the action of kinesins that slide apart antiparallel microtubules in vitro.
source: Thus, if present in excess, Ase1 resists spindle elongation. This is consistent with previous in vitro studies where Ase1 has been shown to act as a brake, opposing the action of kinesins, which slide apart antiparallel microtubules (Braun et al., 2011; Lansky et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Braun et al., 2011; Lansky et al., 2015).

claim: There is no significant difference in anaphase B spindle elongation between wild-type and ase1off cells.
source: However, we could not observe a significant difference in anaphase B spindle elongation between wild-type and ase1off cells (Figure 6F and H), even though Ase1-GFP intensities at the midzone were strongly diminished (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6F, H and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ase1 does not promote or oppose spindle elongation in anaphase when expressed at endogenous levels.
source: Together, with regards to velocity, Ase1 does not promote or oppose spindle elongation in anaphase when expressed at endogenous levels, even though it has been shown to be essential for spindle stability (Janson et al., 2007; Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no significant difference in spindle elongation velocity in ase1off cells, and supported by citations to published research (Janson et al., 2007; Loïodice et al., 2005; Yamashita et al., 2005).

claim: Deletion of pkl1 alone does not affect anaphase B elongation velocity.
source: Since the absence of Pkl1 alone does not affect elongation velocity (Figure 6H), this decrease may result from the absence of Cut7.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: Double deletion of pkl1 and cut7 results in a slight but significant decrease in anaphase velocity compared to wild-type cells.
source: Comparing anaphase velocity with wild-type cells showed a slight but significant decrease (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: Cut7 is required to promote spindle elongation in Anaphase B to a small extent.
source: Therefore, Cut7 does not act as a brake in fission yeast and might in the opposite be required to promote spindle elongation in Anaphase B, to a small extent, as previously suggested (Rincon et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing decreased velocity in pkl1Δcut7Δ cells and supported by a citation to published research (Rincon et al., 2017).

claim: Deletion of klp2 does not significantly alter anaphase B elongation velocity.
source: However, its deletion did not significantly alter anaphase B elongation velocity either (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6H.

claim: The length of Klp9-GFP signal increases in cdc25-22 cells compared to wild-type and wee1-50 cells.
source: Line scan-analysis of Klp9-GFP signals at anaphase spindles in wee1-50, wild-type and cdc25-22 cells revealed an increase in signal length in cdc25-22 cells compared to wild-type and wee1-50 cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: The length of microtubule overlap increases in longer spindles.
source: This indicates, that the length of microtubule overlap increases in longer spindles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing increased Klp9-GFP signal length in longer spindles.

claim: Midzone length correlates strongly with spindle length with R2 = 0.82 and slope m = 0.26.
source: Indeed, midzone length, measured by the length of increased mCherry-Atb2 fluorescence at the center of the spindle in a kymograph (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), correlated strongly with spindle length (Figure 7B: R2 = 0.82, m = 0.26).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In wee1-50 cells the mean midzone length is 2.6 ± 0.4 µm.
source: In wee1-50 cells the mean midzone length was 2.6 ± 0.4 µm, while it measured 3.2 ± 0.5 µm in wild-type and 5.0 ± 0.6 µm in cdc25-22 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In wild-type cells the mean midzone length is 3.2 ± 0.5 µm.
source: In wee1-50 cells the mean midzone length was 2.6 ± 0.4 µm, while it measured 3.2 ± 0.5 µm in wild-type and 5.0 ± 0.6 µm in cdc25-22 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In cdc25-22 cells the mean midzone length is 5.0 ± 0.6 µm.
source: In wee1-50 cells the mean midzone length was 2.6 ± 0.4 µm, while it measured 3.2 ± 0.5 µm in wild-type and 5.0 ± 0.6 µm in cdc25-22 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The midzone length is kept rather constant throughout the progression of spindle elongation.
source: Furthermore, the midzone length, while fluctuating, was kept rather constant throughout the progression of spindle elongation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The microtubule growth rate is largely correlated to anaphase B spindle elongation.
source: This indicates, that the microtubule growth rate is largely correlated to anaphase B spindle elongation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing constant midzone length during spindle elongation.

claim: Microtubule density at the midzone slightly increases with spindle length with R2 = 0.53 and slope m = 18.36.
source: Microtubule density, examined by the mCherry-Atb2 intensity value of a fixed area at the midzone region, slightly increased with spindle length (Figure 7C: R2 = 0.53, m = 18.36) whereas values are significantly different between wee1-50, wild-type and cdc25-22 cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 7C.

claim: The ratio of tubulin intensity of the anaphase spindle and spindle length scales with cell size.
source: The increased microtubule density of longer spindles is moreover suggested by the fact, that the ratio of tubulin intensity of the anaphase spindle and spindle length, giving the tubulin intensity per unit length of the spindle, scaled with cell size (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Total mCherry-Atb2 intensity of the whole length of the midzone increases strongly proportional to spindle length with R2 = 0.82 and slope m = 92.22.
source: Taking both parameters, overlap length and density, into account by measuring the total mCherry-Atb2 intensity of the whole length of the midzone, we observed a strong increase proportional to spindle length (Figure 7D: R2 = 0.82, m = 92.22).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis presented in Figure 7D.

claim: Longer spindles provide more binding sites for Klp9 by forming longer regions of antiparallel overlapping microtubules and by bundling more microtubules within this region.
source: Thus, longer spindles provide much more binding sites for Klp9 by forming longer regions of antiparallel overlapping microtubules and by bundling more microtubules within this region (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing increased midzone length and microtubule density in longer spindles, and supported by Figure 7E.

claim: The ratio of Klp9-GFP intensity and total mCherry-Atb2 intensity of the midzone decreases with spindle length.
source: Interestingly, the ratio of Klp9-GFP intensity and total mCherry-Atb2 intensity of the midzone, which we use as an estimate for the occupancy of the midzone with motors, decreased with spindle length (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 7F.

claim: The midzone of longer spindles might be less occupied with Klp9 molecules in relation to shorter spindles in smaller cells.
source: Hence, within larger cells the midzone of longer spindles might be less occupied with Klp9 molecules in relation to shorter spindles in smaller cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing decreased ratio of Klp9-GFP intensity to mCherry-Atb2 intensity with increasing spindle length.

claim: Spindle length scales with cell size in fission yeast.
source: Our results show that spindle length scales with cell size in fission yeast, and that mitosis duration, defined from spindle assembly to disassembly, is constant irrespective of cell and spindle size (Figures 1, 2 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1, 2 and 8.

claim: Mitosis duration is constant irrespective of cell and spindle size in fission yeast.
source: Our results show that spindle length scales with cell size in fission yeast, and that mitosis duration, defined from spindle assembly to disassembly, is constant irrespective of cell and spindle size (Figures 1, 2 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1, 2 and 8.

claim: Kinesin-6 Klp9 adjusts the velocity of spindle elongation in Anaphase B to keep mitosis duration constant.
source: We reveal that the kinesin-6 Klp9 is an essential player in fixing a constant duration of mitosis in cells of different sizes through adjusting the velocity of spindle elongation in Anaphase B (Figures 3 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: Cut7 alone does not promote the establishment of a cell-size dependent spindle elongation velocity.
source: In this background, the mitotic spindle can still elongate, due to the presence of the kinesin-5 Cut7 (Rincon et al., 2017), but Cut7 alone does not promote the establishment of a cell-size dependent spindle elongation velocity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that klp9Δ cells have similar velocities regardless of cell size, and supported by a citation to published research (Rincon et al., 2017).

claim: The more Klp9 is available, the more it is recruited to the spindle and the faster the spindle is elongated.
source: Intensity measurements and overexpression of Klp9 demonstrated that the more Klp9 is available, the more it is recruited to the spindle and the faster the spindle is elongated (Figures 4, 5 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4, 5 and 8.

claim: The force produced by several full-length Xenopus kinesin-5 molecules depends linearly on the motor number in vitro.
source: Similarly, the force produced by several full-length Xenopus kinesin-5, that crosslink and slide apart two antiparallel microtubules, has been shown to depend linearly on the motor number in vitro (Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Shimamoto et al., 2015).

claim: Forces generated by kinesin-1 molecules do not scale with motor number in vitro.
source: Similarly, in contrast to Xenopus kinesin-5 (Shimamoto et al., 2015), forces generated by kinesin-1 molecules do not scale with motor number in vitro (Furuta et al., 2013; Jamison et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Furuta et al., 2013; Jamison et al., 2012; Shimamoto et al., 2015).

claim: TPX2 slows down MT-sliding of Eg5 but not of kinesin-1 in vitro.
source: Such a differential regulation has been reported for the MAP TPX2 and the kinesin-5 Eg5. In vitro TPX2 slowed down MT-sliding of Eg5 but not of kinesin-1 (Ma et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ma et al., 2011).

claim: The force generated by ensembles of full-length Xenopus kinesin-5 scales with the number of motors bound and the overlap length in vitro.
source: Accordingly, the force generated by ensembles of full-length Xenopus kinesin-5 scales with the number of motors bound and the overlap length in vitro (Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Shimamoto et al., 2015).

claim: The sliding velocity of antiparallel oriented microtubules scales with the initial overlap length in vitro using PRC1 and Kif4A.
source: Moreover, in vitro studies using the Ase1 homolog PRC1 and the plus-end directed motor Kif4A showed that the sliding velocity of antiparallel oriented microtubules scales with the initial overlap length (Wijeratne and Subramanian, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Wijeratne and Subramanian, 2018).

claim: At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, spindles in wild-type S. pombe cells consist of about nine microtubules.
source: This is consistent with EM-based electron tomographic reconstructions of wild-type S. pombe spindles (Ward et al., 2014) and serial-section reconstructions of cdc25-22 spindles (Ding et al., 1993). At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, spindles in wild-type cells consist of about nine microtubules and cdc25-22 spindles contain approximately sixteen microtubules (Ding et al., 1993; Ward et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ward et al., 2014; Ding et al., 1993).

claim: cdc25-22 spindles contain approximately sixteen microtubules at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: This is consistent with EM-based electron tomographic reconstructions of wild-type S. pombe spindles (Ward et al., 2014) and serial-section reconstructions of cdc25-22 spindles (Ding et al., 1993). At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, spindles in wild-type cells consist of about nine microtubules and cdc25-22 spindles contain approximately sixteen microtubules (Ding et al., 1993; Ward et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ding et al., 1993; Ward et al., 2014).

claim: Increasing motor densities of kinesin-8 reduce motor velocity.
source: Indeed, increasing motor densities, for instance of kinesin-8, have been reported to reduce motor velocity (Leduc et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Leduc et al., 2012).

claim: As motors enter a region of high motor density, their velocity is slowed down, potentially due to steric interference.
source: As motors entered a region of high motor density, their velocity was slowed down, potentially due to steric interference.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from observations of motor behavior in high density regions.

claim: Increasing densities of Cut7 immobilized on a coverslip decrease the sliding velocity of attached microtubules.
source: Similarly, increasing densities of Cut7, immobilized on a coverslip, decreased the sliding velocity of attached microtubules (Britto et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Britto et al., 2016).

claim: Antiparallel microtubules organized in the spindle midzone grow constantly in Ptk1 cells and diatom spindles.
source: The fact that the overlap length did not shrink during spindle elongation, suggests that the associated microtubules grow constantly, as reported for Ptk1 cells and diatom spindles (Cande, 1986; Cande and McDonald, 1985; Masuda and Cande, 1987; Saxton and McIntosh, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Cande, 1986; Cande and McDonald, 1985; Masuda and Cande, 1987; Saxton and McIntosh, 1987).

claim: In Drosophila embryos, depletion of kinesin-8 KLP67A increased the velocity of microtubule sliding and anaphase B spindle elongation.
source: Accordingly, in Drosophila embryos depletion of the kinesin-8 KLP67A, which is thought to trigger microtubule plus-end depolymerization (Varga et al., 2009; Varga et al., 2006), increased the velocity of microtubule sliding and thus of anaphase B spindle elongation (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Wang et al., 2010; Varga et al., 2009; Varga et al., 2006).

claim: Kinesin-5 may act as a MT polymerase.
source: The kinesin-6 could achieve this role by either acting as a MT polymerase itself, as it has been suggested for the other MT sliding motor kinesin-5 (Chen and Hancock, 2015) or by recruiting other spindle components that regulate microtubule polymerization.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chen and Hancock, 2015).

claim: Reducing the microtubule growth rate by disrupting the interaction between Mal3 and Dis1 results in slightly faster spindle elongation in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast, reducing the microtubule growth rate by disrupting the interaction between Mal3, an EB1 protein, and Dis1, a member of the XMAP215/TOG family, resulted in a slightly faster spindle elongation (Matsuo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Matsuo et al., 2016).

claim: Larger cells provide more Klp9 molecules resulting in the recruitment of more motors to the spindle midzone.
source: To conclude, we propose a model in which larger cells provide more Klp9 molecules resulting in the recruitment of more motors to the spindle midzone (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on experimental data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: An increased amount of motors at the midzone accelerates the velocity of spindle elongation.
source: An increased amount of motors at the midzone accelerates the velocity of spindle elongation, either by increasing the velocity of microtubule sliding or by increasing the rate of microtubule growth.
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on experimental data and inference.

claim: The effect of increased motor amounts on spindle elongation velocity may be enhanced by a lower rate of molecular crowding on longer spindles.
source: In addition, this effect may be enhanced by a lower rate of molecular crowding on longer spindles (Figure 8: lower panel).
evidence: The claim is a proposed mechanism based on experimental data and speculation, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Cell-size-dependent spindle elongation velocity may be a consequence of scaling of essential spindle components with cell size.
source: Cumulatively, this study suggests that cell-size-dependent spindle elongation velocity, which ultimately ensures a constant mitotic time frame in cells of various sizes, may be a consequence of scaling of essential spindle components or parameters with cell size: the number of Klp9 molecules, microtubule density and midzone length (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on experimental data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: The constant mitotic time frame could be regulated by the cytoplasmic volume.
source: We thus wonder if, like spindle length (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013), the constant mitotic time frame could be regulated by the cytoplasmic volume.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on analogy to spindle length regulation, supported by citations to published research (Good et al., 2013; Hazel et al., 2013).

claim: The concentration of tubulin and Klp9 is constant in fission yeast cells of different sizes.
source: Consistent with this model we found the concentration of tubulin and Klp9 to be constant in fission yeast cells of different sizes.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Larger cells provide more tubulin and Klp9 molecules.
source: With an unaltered concentration, total amounts increase proportionally to cell size: larger cells provide more tubulin and Klp9 molecules (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: In various human cell lines, the duration of G1-, S- and G2-phase varied widely while mitosis duration was remarkably constant.
source: It was previously reported that in various human cell lines the duration of G1-, S- and G2-phase varied widely while mitosis duration was remarkably constant (Araujo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Araujo et al., 2016).

claim: Mammalian cells spend 20–60 min in mitosis with an average of 45 min in various human cell lines.
source: Mammalian cells spend 20–60 min in mitosis (Yang et al., 2008) with an average of 45 min in various human cell lines (Araujo et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Yang et al., 2008; Araujo et al., 2016).

claim: Fission yeast spends approximately 30 min in mitosis.
source: Fission yeast spends approximately 30 min in mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Interphase duration accounts for 12–30 hr in mammalian cells.
source: In contrast, interphase duration accounts for 12–30 hr in mammalian cells (Ganem and Pellman, 2012; Yang et al., 2008), but only for around 3 hr in S. pombe cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ganem and Pellman, 2012; Yang et al., 2008).

claim: Interphase duration accounts for around 3 hr in S. pombe cells.
source: In contrast, interphase duration accounts for 12–30 hr in mammalian cells (Ganem and Pellman, 2012; Yang et al., 2008), but only for around 3 hr in S. pombe cells.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about S. pombe cell cycle.
